edits.find: TSH first: low TSH + high T4 = thyrotoxicosis; high TSH + low T4 = primary hypothyroidism; both low = central. Then RAIU splits thyrotoxicosis: high uptake = the gland is MAKING hormone; low uptake = leaking or exogenous, where antithyroid drugs are useless.
edits.with: Check TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) first. Low TSH with high T4 (thyroxine) is thyrotoxicosis. High TSH with low T4 is primary hypothyroidism. Both low means central hypothyroidism. In thyrotoxicosis, RAIU (radioactive iodine uptake) is the next step. High uptake means the gland is making hormone. Low uptake means the hormone is leaking from the gland or is exogenous; antithyroid drugs are useless there.

edits.find:
When a stem describes an illness and says the patient "remains on medication" without naming it, the question is a two-step inference: identify the drug class the illness requires, then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. Psychosis → antipsychotic → the one with the highest prolactin liability.

The number is the discriminator. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. A level of 70 assassinates the prolactinoma option without any imaging.
edits.with:
When a patient with a known illness remains on an unnamed medication, identify the drug by two-step inference. First identify the drug class the illness requires. Then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. In psychosis, the class is an antipsychotic, and the member is the one with the highest prolactin liability.

The prolactin level separates drug-induced hyperprolactinemia from prolactinoma. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. In this patient, a level of 70 is in the drug-induced range and excludes prolactinoma without any imaging.

edits.find: Dopamine is prolactin-inhibiting factor; D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes that inhibition. Highest prolactin effect: risperidone and paliperidone, plus high-potency typicals like haloperidol. Lowest: aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist that can lower prolactin), quetiapine, clozapine — which makes aripiprazole the answer to both "least likely to cause this" and "what should you switch to."

edits.find: Elevated prolactin → pregnancy test, TSH, medication review, renal function → only if all negative → MRI pituitary. Don't image before excluding the cheap causes. Hook effect: a very large prolactinoma can saturate the assay and give a falsely low value — repeat with dilution. And prolactinoma is the pituitary tumor you treat medically: dopamine agonists (cabergoline > bromocriptine) are first-line even for macroadenomas because they shrink the tumor; surgery is for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy.

edits.find:
DXA at age 65 for all women — or earlier if she has ≥1 risk factor (prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, low BMI, chronic glucocorticoids). Run the risk-factor list before applying the age default. A patient with timely menopause and an empty list waits until 65.

⚠︎ Two ledgers. The rule above is the exam ledger and the operational shorthand. The USPSTF statement expresses the same idea quantitatively: screen before 65 when a FRAX-estimated 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk reaches that of a 65-year-old with no risk factors (~9.3%). The exam scores the risk-factor list; know FRAX for the clinic and for questions that hand you a percentage. Fully worked in the board-style brief DEXA: When Screening Starts Early.

The most common time-waster here: obesity is protective for osteoporosis, not a risk factor. The risk factor is low body weight (<58 kg / 127 lb) — higher weight increases bone density through mechanical loading and peripheral aromatization to estrogen.
edits.with:
Screen all women with DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) at age 65. Screen earlier if she has ≥1 risk factor: prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, low BMI (body mass index) or chronic glucocorticoids. Check the risk-factor list before applying the age default. A patient with timely menopause and no risk factors waits until 65.

⚠︎ The rule above is the exam answer and the operational shorthand. The USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) statement expresses the same idea quantitatively. Screen before 65 when the FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk reaches that of a 65-year-old with no risk factors (~9.3%). The exam answer uses the risk-factor list; use FRAX in clinical practice and when a percentage is given. The board-style brief DEXA: When Screening Starts Early works this through in full.

Obesity is protective for osteoporosis, not a risk factor. Low body weight (<58 kg / 127 lb) is the risk factor. Higher weight increases bone density through mechanical loading and peripheral aromatization to estrogen.
